mainEntity.name: How long should a dental crown last before needing replacement?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dental crowns are designed to be long-lasting restorations, and with appropriate care, many crowns function well for ten to fifteen years or longer. However, longevity varies depending on the crown material, the patient's bite, oral hygiene habits, and whether teeth grinding is present. Some patients require earlier replacement due to decay at the margin, changes in the gum line, or aesthetic preferences. Regular dental check-ups allow your dentist to monitor the condition of existing crowns and advise you on timing should replacement become necessary.

Crown replacement is typically carried out under local anaesthetic, so the procedure itself should not be painful. Patients may experience some sensitivity or mild discomfort in the days following the appointment, particularly if additional tooth preparation or decay removal was required. This usually settles within a few days. If you experience persistent or worsening pain after a crown procedure, it is advisable to contact your dental practice so the tooth can be re-evaluated.

mainEntity.name: Can a crown be replaced on a tooth that has had root canal treatment?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, a crown can be replaced on a root-treated tooth, though the clinical approach may differ slightly. Root-treated teeth are often supported by a post and core build-up, which provides the foundation for the crown. Before replacing the crown, your dentist will assess the integrity of the post and core, the condition of the root, and the surrounding bone and gum tissue. This ensures that the replacement crown has a sound and stable foundation. Clinical assessment will determine whether any preparatory work is needed before the new crown is placed.

mainEntity.name: Is there a risk of damaging the tooth further during crown replacement?

acceptedAnswer.text: Careful clinical technique significantly reduces the risk of damage during crown replacement. Before removal of the existing crown, your dentist will assess the tooth and plan the procedure appropriately. In some cases, an existing crown can be cut away to preserve as much tooth structure as possible. As with any dental procedure, there are inherent clinical considerations, and your dentist will discuss these with you during your consultation. Any risks are balanced against the clinical need for replacement and are managed with care and precision.

mainEntity.name: What happens if there is not enough tooth structure left for a new crown?

acceptedAnswer.text: If the remaining tooth structure is insufficient to support a new crown, your dentist may discuss options such as placing a core build-up using dental composite to restore the necessary volume before the crown is fitted. In some cases, where the tooth is significantly compromised, other treatment options may need to be considered. The decision will always be based on a clinical assessment of the tooth's restorability and the patient's overall oral health. Your dentist will explain all options clearly so that you can make an informed decision.

mainEntity.name: Is it possible to have a temporary crown fitted while waiting for the permanent replacement?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, a temporary crown is routinely placed after tooth preparation to protect the tooth while the permanent crown is being fabricated in the dental laboratory. This temporary restoration maintains the tooth's appearance and function and helps protect the prepared surface and surrounding gum tissue. Temporary crowns are not designed to be long-term solutions, so it is important to attend the follow-up appointment to have the permanent crown fitted within the timeframe recommended by your dentist.
